module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Conjectures associated with A109909

$a(n)$ = number of primes of the form $k(n-k)-1$.

*References:*
- [A109909](https://oeis.org/A109909)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace OeisA109909

/--
$a(n)$ is the number of primes of the form $k(n-k)-1$.
This counts the number of distinct prime values in the set $\{k(n-k)-1 | 1 \le k < n\}$.
-/
def a (n : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.Ico 1 n).image (fun k => k * (n - k) - 1)
  |>.filter Nat.Prime
  |>.card

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_1 : a 1 = 0 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_2 : a 2 = 0 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_3 : a 3 = 0 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_4 : a 4 = 2 := by decide

@[category test, AMS 11]
theorem a_5 : a 5 = 2 := by decide

/--
Conjecture: $a(n) > 0$ for $n > 3$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem conjecture : ∀ n > 3, a n > 0 := by
  sorry

end OeisA109909

reformulations.difference: The source says "primes of the form k*(n-k)-1" and does not restrict k. The Lean definition `a` takes k from `Finset.Ico 1 n` only, computes `k * (n - k) - 1` with truncated ℕ subtraction, and counts distinct prime values. The OEIS programs, as in the sibling entries, count k in 1..n/2 instead.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: When 1 ≤ k < n we have n - k ≥ 1 and k(n-k) ≥ 1, so neither ℕ subtraction truncates. The value equals the integer k(n-k)-1. For any integer k ≤ 0 or k ≥ n, k(n-k)-1 ≤ -1, so it is never a positive prime. Restricting k to [1, n) therefore loses nothing. On [1, ⌊n/2⌋], k ↦ k(n-k) is strictly increasing, since k'(n-k') - k(n-k) = (k'-k)(n-k-k') > 0, and it is symmetric under k ↔ n-k. So the number of distinct prime values equals the number of k ≤ n/2 that give a prime, and the two counting conventions agree. The Lean `a` matches all 93 b-file terms exactly. In any case, `a n > 0` only asks whether some k gives a prime, so the conjecture does not depend on how the primes are counted. I proved two facts in Lean: `a n > 0 ↔ ∃ k, 1 ≤ k ∧ k < n ∧ (k * (n - k) - 1).Prime`, and `(∀ n > 3, a n > 0) ↔ ∀ n > 3, ∃ k : ℤ, (k*(n-k)-1).natAbs.Prime ∧ 0 < k*(n-k)-1`.

review.notes:
No findings. All declarations were checked. The definition `a` matches every OEIS b-file term exactly (n = 1..93, checked with `#eval`). Tests a_1..a_5 match the OEIS data 0, 0, 0, 2, 2. `conjecture` (`∀ n > 3, a n > 0`) states the OEIS comment verbatim, and the bound is tight because a(3) = 0. A C search found no counterexample for 4 ≤ n ≤ 10^6. OEIS separately records verification up to 10^9 (Mauro Fiorentini, 2023). For n ≤ 2000, a(n) = 1 only at n = 6, 8, 10, 20, 22, 40.

On status: since 2024 the OEIS entry links an unpublished ResearchGate preprint, Pengcheng Niu and Junli Zhang, "On Two Conjectures of A. Murthy" (DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.16430.11848). ResearchGate blocked me, so I could not read what it claims. OpenAlex and DataCite record it as an unpublished preprint, not accepted, with zero citations. The OEIS entry still calls the claim a conjecture, and the edit history adds the link without any note. I therefore see no status issue with `research open`. If the preprint claims a full proof, maintainers may want to look at it. Such a proof would need a special case of Hardy–Littlewood-type results: for even n = 2m the conjecture says m^2 - 1 is a prime plus a square. An unreviewed preprint does not meet the repository's 'informally accepted' bar.

The sibling file OEIS/109908.lean states the logically equivalent conjecture for A109908 in the same way.
